source.title: Mood Matters: How Syntactic Sensitivity Undermines Safety Alignment
source.authors: Alina Klerings; Jannik Brinkmann; Heiner Stuckenschmidt; Simone Ponzetto

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper refines the refusal-mechanism account by showing that syntactic features causally affect refusal, alongside evidence that harmfulness recognition remains stable across syntax. It does not directly ablate or add the difference-in-means refusal direction.
record.gate_note: The paper uses a precomputed difference-in-means refusal direction as a scalar readout, but steers upstream SAE features rather than ablating or adding that direction itself. Behavioral rates across syntax, centroid-probe results, feature-steering outcomes, and SFT training/evaluation results are recorded. Values used only to select SAE features or steering coefficients are omitted.
record.test_reason: In a new setting (syntactic rephrasing of harmful requests), the study's results bear on V5. Centroid probes show harmfulness stays decodable across syntax at about 70%, while refusal behaviour (ASR@10) shifts strongly with syntax. That is a dissociation between harm encoding and the refusal decision. The study never ablates or adds the difference-in-means direction: it uses the direction's projection only as a readout for steering upstream SAE features. So V1–V4 and V6–V8 are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also stress that harm recognition stays intact internally, so refusal failure comes from a confounding syntactic signal. They call syntax a necessary but not sufficient condition for refusal. They claim diverse SFT works without degrading capabilities, though MMLU fell from 62.85 to 59.80.
record.recipe_differences: Rather than ablating or adding the difference-in-means refusal direction, the paper uses its projection as a readout and steers upstream SAE features; it also evaluates syntax variation, centroid probes, and SFT data variation.
record.method_sensitivity: Refusal and attack success vary substantially with syntactic form. Feature-steering effects differ between harmful and benign prompts; the paper also reports that syntax-diverse SFT does not improve declarative cases and increases imperative ASR in the reported run.

fits_no_version.finding: Steering upstream syntax-sensitive SAE features flips refusal. In Gemma-2 2B, feature 3347 gives 100% compliance-to-refusal on harmful non-imperative prompts, against 18% for random latents. The same steering flips benign prompts less often (Gemma 48.8–65.5%, Qwen 57.5%, Llama 43.6%).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Upstream syntax features causally drive the refusal signal, jointly with harmfulness.

fits_no_version.finding: Syntax-diverse safety SFT lowers ASR for six of eight syntax forms but raises it for imperative prompts (0.23 vs 0.00).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal generalization across syntax depends on the syntactic diversity of the safety training data.

fits_no_version.finding: Capability scores after the different SFT runs (MMLU drops about 3 points with Syntax-Mix).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Syntax-diverse safety SFT has a small capability cost.

fits_no_version.finding: Post-training corpora are biased toward imperative mood and active voice, and imperative phrasing alone does not trigger refusal on clearly benign prompts.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Syntactic bias in post-training data, plus a harm signal, conditions refusal.

record.problems: The main behavioral evaluation uses 100 harmful and 100 benign English prompts. The causal feature-steering study focuses on Gemma-2 (2B), and SAE labels are heuristic. The paper reports manual annotation of 120 responses with 91.7% agreement and Cohen’s Kappa of 83.4. The main cross-model ASR results are largely presented in figures; the SFT experiment uses a 10% sample of the training corpus and one epoch.
record.rows_left_out: The individual model-by-syntax ASR@10 values and detailed per-variant probe accuracies are shown in Figures 3, 4, 7, and 8; they were not transcribed where the supplied text did not state exact values. Additional steering-feature results in Table 13 and related plots were not separately recorded to stay within the 60-row limit and because the table is flattened and aggregates variants.

untested.parts: No ablation or addition of the difference-in-means direction. The direction (Arditi's, at layer 15 for Gemma-2 2B; computed for Qwen and Llama) is used only as a scalar readout R.
The study does not report whether syntactic jailbreaks lower the projection onto the refusal direction, and it does no training against ablation.
No analysis of the number or geometry of refusal directions.
No test of transfer across languages, model variants or base-to-instruct models; the evaluation is English only.
The SFT experiments vary the syntax of the safety data but never test whether a removable direction exists.

missing.what: Projection R onto the refusal direction per syntax form, before steering. This could bear on V3, since it would show whether syntactic jailbreaks lower the refusal-direction projection. The text gives no numeric values.
Per-model probe accuracies by syntax form for the other models

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V4 links were wrong: upstream-feature steering does not test refusal-direction geometry. The V5 verdict rests on the probe-versus-ASR dissociation, not on the steering flip rates.

versions.untested_parts: No direct ablation or addition of the difference-in-means refusal direction; no test of whether removing it at every layer and position eliminates refusal while preserving general abilities.
No test of attacks suppressing the refusal direction or training against its ablation.
Tests causal influence from syntax-sensitive upstream features, not whether refusal is geometrically an affine region or cone, nor the number or geometry of refusal directions.

Tests harmfulness centroid-probe performance across syntax and contrasts harmful with benign prompts during steering; does not fully characterize or localize distinct harmfulness and refusal representations.
No cross-language, base-to-instruct, or model-variant transfer test of the refusal direction.
Training interventions test syntax-conditioned refusal, not whether training determines the existence of a removable refusal direction.

rows.subject: Gemma-2 (2B)
rows.operation_detail: Steered feature 3347 in layer 5 positively on harmful prompts in non-imperative forms to induce refusal.
rows.value: 100% on all harmful prompts in non-imperative form
rows.note: The paper reports the aggregate result across non-imperative variants.
rows.check: Steering an upstream syntax SAE feature measures what drives refusal. It says nothing about whether refusal is one direction, affine or a cone, so the V4 link is wrong.

rows.subject: Gemma-2 (2B)
rows.operation_detail: Steered feature 3347 positively to induce refusal on benign prompts.
rows.note: The authors say the effect on benign prompts is less effective than on harmful prompts; the text gives this range across syntax variants.
rows.check: This is the same upstream-feature steering on benign prompts. It is not a refusal-geometry test (V4), and it does not compare separate harm and refusal encodings (V5).

rows.subject: Gemma-2 (2B)
rows.operation_detail: Steered feature 3347 negatively on imperative prompts to suppress refusal.
rows.note: The paper describes these as harmless-compliance responses and says removing the syntactic trigger can cross the refusal boundary in some cases.
rows.check: This is upstream-feature suppression, not ablation of the refusal direction or a test of its geometry, so the V4 link is wrong. Of the 23% flips, only 8% are harmful compliance (Table 1).

rows.subject: Gemma-2 (2B)

rows.check: This is the random-latent control for the feature-steering experiment and has no bearing on V4.

relation.reason: Its own probing and ASR results bear on V5. The Arditi direction is otherwise used only as a readout (projection R) for SAE feature discovery and steering, with no ablation or addition test of V1.

tranche.reason: New setting (syntactic rephrasings of JBB harmful prompts) with a result bearing on V5: harm stays decodable while refusal fails. Nothing in the text argues that a version is wrong or needs restating, so the reader's earlier T5 is not supported.

source_check.notes: The probe uses centroids averaged over layers and tokens. Accuracy is about 70% against JBB's 'seemingly harmful' benign prompts, which is modest above chance. The causal part is SAE steering on Gemma-2 2B: feature 3347 gives 100% induced refusal vs 18.21% for random latents, but only 8% harmful compliance when suppressed. The 'only 8% harmful compliance' example passage and the synthetic-data prompt are quoted method material, not instructions.

statements.correction: Centroid-probe accuracy around 70%, with no meaningful within- vs cross-syntax difference: Qwen-2.5 7B, Gemma-2 27B, Llama-3.3 70B (Figure 4), similar trends in more models (Figure 7). Probes are trained on 70% of imperative prompts, averaged over layers and token positions. Worst-case Delta-max ASR@10 runs from +15% (Tulu-3 70B) to +71% (Apertus 8B), with the conditional form worst for all 16 instruct models (7B-70B, 8 families) and 95% paired-bootstrap CIs. Gemma-2 2B is used only for SAE steering (Delta-max ASR@10 +60%).
statements.problem: Puts the ~70% centroid-probe accuracy on Gemma-2 2B, but the text reports it for Qwen-2.5 7B, Gemma-2 27B and Llama-3.3 70B (Fig. 4) plus more models in Fig. 7. Gemma-2 2B has no probe result. The ASR range, Tulu-3 70B low end, 16 models, CIs and code are right.
